Discover UK employment guidance for Statutory Sick Pay: waiting days. Task relevance is separate from current law, commencement and a need to edit.

passages.quote:
de of the EU, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland that the UK has a social security agreement with

The UK has social security agreements with countries which are sometimes called Reciprocal agreements or Double Contribution Conventions.

If the employee has a certificate issued by another country which states they are subject to that country’s social security legislation, you can accept this as proof that the employee does not have to pay UK National Insurance contributions for the period covered by the certificate.

Leave the National Insurance letters and values fields blank for that employee.

Employees coming to work in the UK from any other country

You and these employees are exempt from paying UK National Insurance contributions for the first 52 weeks of their employment here provided that:

they’re not ordinarily resident in the UK

they normally work outside the UK for a foreign employer

they’re sent to work in the UK for a time by that foreign employer

when in the UK they continue to work for that employer

Leave the National Insurance letters and values fields blank for that employee.

Modified PAYE arrangements

If you’ve an agreement with HMRC to operate an Employment Procedures (EP) Appendix 6 scheme, only one FPS is needed each month, irrespective of the number of payments made either in the UK or overseas. The FPS must include one month’s portion of the total grossed up estimated cash and non-cash earnings for the year.

The estimated pay including all estimated benefits in kind is reported in the ‘Taxable Pay to Date’ and ‘Taxable Pay in this Period’ fields.

No entries are needed in the fields:

Benefits Taxed via Payroll

Benefits Subject to Class 1 NIC

Benefits Not Subject to Class1 NIC

Most EP Appendix 6 payrolls are shadow payrolls used to account for tax and National Insurance contributions only.

Any elements of UK pay, must not be included in the FPS for the local payroll as this may create duplicate records. These payments must be made outside payroll.

Where the EP Appendix 6 scheme is based on actual rather than estimated pay and is used to deliver earnings, the ‘Deductions from Net Pay’ field should be used as necessary.

Under the Modified PAYE arrangement in Appendix 6, employers prepare a best estimate of cash earnings and non-cash benefits at the beginning of each tax year. The best estimate may also take into account provisional relief for overseas workdays.

From 6 April 2025, overseas workday relief will be subject to an annual limit in each qualifying year and consideration should be given to how the employee’s estimated pay will interact with this limit.

You can continue to pay the tax and National Insurance contributions quarterly if you have 5 or fewer employees, but you will need to contact HMRC before switching to quarterly payments.

For employees who have left the UK during the tax year, in accordance with EP Appendix 6, set the irregular payment pattern indicator and leave the employee record open until the month 12 adjustment is made. The actual date of leaving will be entered with month 12 figures on the month 12 FPS.

If you’ve a linked agreement for National Insurance contributions under EP Appendix 7A you must include the National Insurance contributions on the estimated pay on the FPS with the tax each month under the EP Appendix 6 scheme.

Payments

Non-UK bank accounts

Amounts paid into overseas accounts should be reported in the data field value of deductions from net pay in the period. This will make sure that the amount paid into the UK bank account is correctly confirmed by the Bacs hash code.

Made by the overseas employer

Tax and National Insurance contributions must be calculated and reported for the correct pay period. Corrections to previous month’s payments for irregular payments and foreign taxes both paid by the overseas employer, can be reported by submitting an additional FPS or revised year-to-date figures on the current FPS.

Work done in and outside the UK

Special rules apply for globally mobile employees. An employee is a globally mobile employee if they work in and outside the UK during a tax year in which they:

are not resident in the UK

are UK resident and eligible for split year treatment

are UK resident and are a qualifying new resident

You can work out residence in a tax year using the statutory residence test. An employee is a qualifying new resident for tax year if all of the following apply:

they’re UK resident in the tax year

have been non-UK resident for a continuous period of at least 10 tax years immediately prior to that tax year

they’re not disqualified for the tax year

An employee who is a qualifying new resident for a tax year will remain so in any tax year during the following 3 year period in which they’re UK resident, so that they can be a qualifying new resident in up to 4 tax years.

If you’re the employer of a globally mobile employee, you can tell HMRC that you’ll operate PAYE on a proportion of an employee’s income.

You can also send a notification for employees who are treated as non-resident in the UK for the purposes of applying a Double Taxation Agreement.

If you’ve sent us a notification and HMRC has acknowledged receipt, you must include only the specified proportion of any payment the notification applies to on the FPS in the ‘Taxable Pay to Date’ and ‘Taxable Pay in this Period’ fields.

Enter the full employment income the National Insurance contributions are worked out on in the ‘Pay subject to NICs in this Pay Period’ field.

If any part of the pay is paid using the Bacs system, the net pay must be balanced to what is shown in the payroll information by either:

including any payment made outside the Bacs system in the ‘Deductions from Net Pay’ field

adding back any pay not subjected to PAYE tax or National Insurance contributions in the ‘Non Tax or NIC Payment’ field
